analysis.one_liner: Requires drugs developed with taxpayer-funded research to be sold at federally negotiated reasonable prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with 11 cosponsors, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and it died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When federal agencies or nonprofits develop a new drug, biologic, or medical technology using taxpayer-funded research, they often hand the patent to a private company, which can then charge whatever the market will bear. This bill would block that patent handoff until the recipient signs a 'reasonable pricing' agreement with the Department of Health and Human Services. The agreement would guarantee the government pays no more than the lowest price charged in comparable wealthy countries, and would prevent practices that restrict access to Americans. The bill received a hearing from no one: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never taken up before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and patients. The federal government buys huge volumes of prescription drugs through Medicare, Medicaid, and other programs; under this bill it would be charged no more than the lowest price paid by comparable wealthy foreign countries. Patients would also gain from the ban on supply limits or discriminatory terms that restrict Americans' access to taxpayer-funded discoveries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and patients using public health programs

how_it_helps.text: Federal agencies and nonprofits could not hand over a patent on a drug or biologic developed with federally funded research until the recipient agrees to a reasonable pricing deal with HHS [S2][S3].

The government would be charged no more than the lowest price for the same drug among wealthy OECD countries, ending a situation where Americans often pay the highest prices in the developed world [S3].
The pricing formula could not be used to impose supply limits or terms that give foreign purchasers better access than Americans get [S3].
Any waiver from the pricing requirement would require public notice and an opportunity to comment, with a written public-interest finding [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies receiving patents on federally funded drug discoveries, which would face a government-set price ceiling and lose the ability to charge US buyers more than foreign ones. Universities and nonprofit patent holders could also face slower or more complicated licensing deals.

drawbacks.text: Drug companies and many economists argue that price controls on new drugs reduce the incentive to invest in developing the next generation of medicines, since the patent recipient would no longer control pricing (general policy objection, not found in the provided sources).

The bill covers only patents flowing from federally funded research, so its reach depends on how much federal funding actually backs each drug; a company could structure deals to minimize covered inventions, limiting the benefit (inference from the bill's scope as written [S3]).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a narrow but real grievance: taxpayers fund early-stage drug research, then pay some of the world's highest prices for the resulting medicines. For the subset of drugs it covers, the pricing guarantee would directly lower government and possibly patient costs. The main cost is the standard trade-off that lower prices on new drugs may modestly reduce private investment in drug development, and the bill's narrow scope means it would not touch most drugs on the market today.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee, and no one scheduled a hearing or vote before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on October 11, 2019, with 11 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S1][S5].
Three days later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Health, where it remained [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without the committee ever holding a hearing or the House ever voting on the bill [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical companies that license patents on federally funded research keep charging US buyers market rates, including prices above what other wealthy countries pay. Taxpayers and public health programs gained nothing because the pricing requirement never took effect.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring reasonable pricing agreements for taxpayer-funded drug patents.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Health subcommittee, and never took it up before the Congress ended.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Would-be patent recipients and price setters on federally funded drug discoveries
against.what_they_did: Opposed reasonable-pricing mandates of this kind; no pharmaceutical support appears anywhere in the record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record; the bill died in a committee controlled by the House majority, which was Democratic at the time, so it never reached a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would cap what companies can charge for drugs built on taxpayer-funded research and force US prices in line with the lowest foreign prices. Industry's gain from the bill's failure is the public's cost in higher drug prices.

These entities conduct federally funded health research and license the resulting patents; the bill would condition their patent transfers on pricing agreements, possibly complicating licensing revenue but tying public money to public benefit.
